reader.title: Lynching of Lum White's wife and an elderly man near Breckville, Texas
bases: A crowd of men took two Black prisoners from an escort taking them to Carthage and shot them, after a man named Hart had shot Lum White dead at an inquest (A1, A6, A24).

A 'crowd of men' (A1, A6) or 'mob' (A10, A26) seized Lum White's wife and an old man from their escort and shot them, under the accusation that the wife had helped Lum White rape and kill a white girl (A1, A24); the killing of Lum White himself was by one man, Hart (A1).

Every version is a Longview dispatch and the texts are nearly identical, traceable to one special report to the Longview Democrat (A1, A19, A6); no independent local account, inquest or follow-up was found.

summary.text: The lynching of Lum White's wife and an elderly man near Breckville, Texas, took place in October 1881, when a crowd of men took two Black prisoners from an escort bound for Carthage and shot them.
The two had been held after Lum White, a Black man accused of raping and killing a white girl of about fifteen named Sloan, was shot dead at the inquest by a young man named Hart.
A dispatch from Longview carried the story to papers across the country, many of which headlined the alleged crime and presented the killings as vengeance or justice.

According to a special report to the Longview Democrat, condensed in the Dallas Daily Herald under an October 17 dateline, a family named Sloan had recently moved into the neighborhood to pick cotton on the farm of a Mr. Hill.

The report said that Lum White accused the Sloan children of taking peanuts from his patch, and that on a Tuesday he went to the Sloan house intending to whip them but was stopped by Mrs. Sloan and her daughter.

It went on to charge that the next morning, "last Wednesday," White's wife led the daughter to a ravine with a promise of muscadines and held her while Lum White raped her, cut her open and cut her throat.
An inquest was held after the girl's body was found, and there, the report said, the wife "confessed to all of the revolting details."
Hart then shot Lum White dead; a Delaware paper said he "drew a pistol," and a weekly digest said he shot the prisoner "dead in court."
White's wife and "an old negro who lived with them" were then sent under escort toward Carthage.
On the way, "a crowd of men met the escort and took the prisoners and shot them."
Neither the wife nor the old man was named, and no report stated any accusation against the old man beyond his living in the household.
The reports gave no date, hour or exact place for the shooting and no size for the crowd.
No report of an arrest, an inquest on the three dead, or any official action against Hart or the crowd appears in the coverage.

The account first appeared in Texas on October 18 in the Dallas Daily Herald, under the headline "A Horrible Crime Committed by Negroes in East Texas---The Perpetrators Mobbed," and the Dallas Weekly Herald repeated it two days later.
The same report, credited to the Galveston News, ran in the Lake Charles Commercial on October 22 as "The Worst Crime Yet Told—Indiscriminate Lynching."

A St. Louis Republican special from Longview put nearly the same text on the wires on October 19, and it appeared the next day in the Memphis Daily Appeal, both Wheeling dailies and the Rock Island Argus, among others.

The Wheeling Register used "BRUTAL BLACK DEVILS," the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer wrote of "the Summary Vengeance Dealt Them," and the Memphis Daily Appeal said Lum White "Should Have Been Grilled Over a Slow Fire" and that the crime was "Only Partially Punished."
In Austin, the Weekly Democratic Statesman printed a shortened version on October 27 under "SWIFT JUSTICE."
A digest printed on October 26 in the Mower County Transcript and the Watertown Republican said the family was "visited with swift and terrible vengeance by an enraged community."

The South Kentuckian reduced the story to one line, "Three negroes were lynched near Longview, Texas, for the murder of a white girl named Sloan," while a New Hampshire weekly called Hart "a bystander" and said a mob took the prisoners.
The place name varied from paper to paper, appearing as Breckville, Brookville, Brockville, Brickville, Beckville, Breckner and "Lueckville"; the earliest Texas printing gave Breckville.

The Longview dispatches placed the crime on the Wednesday before October 17, a Delaware paper and the weekly digest on "the 12th," and the Morristown Gazette on "the 19th," the date of the St. Louis wire.

The Galveston News version called the family "Lum" and gave the destination as "Courney," the New Hampshire brief said the prisoners were being taken "to jail," and one Pennsylvania copy gave the girl's age as nineteen.

accounts.gist: Long account of the alleged crime; at the inquest the wife confessed, Hart shot Lum White, and a crowd of men met the escort to Carthage and shot the wife and old man.

framing.detail: Dallas Daily Herald: 'A Horrible Crime Committed by Negroes in East Texas---The Perpetrators Mobbed'.
Memphis Daily Appeal: Lum White 'Should Have Been Grilled Over a Slow Fire', crime 'Only Partially Punished'.
Wheeling Daily Intelligencer: 'the Summary Vengeance Dealt Them'; Wheeling Register: 'BRUTAL BLACK DEVILS'.
Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman headed the wire 'SWIFT JUSTICE'.
Lake Charles Commercial (Galveston News): 'The Worst Crime Yet Told—Indiscriminate Lynching'.
Many papers ran the wire under neutral or crime headlines ('A Terrible Death', 'A Shocking Crime', 'The Way They do Murder in Texas').

conflicts.note: OCR and telegraphic variants of one name; the earliest Texas printing (Dallas Herald) gives Breckville.
The 19th is the date of the St. Louis wire; the dispatches agree on a Wednesday before Oct 17.
Courney is likely a misreading of Carthage; the brief's 'to jail' is a paraphrase.
Some versions treat 'Lum' as a surname ('Mrs. Lum').

record_check.dossier: Near Breckville in the earliest Texas printing; Brickville, Brookville, Brockville, Beckville, Breckner and Lueckville elsewhere. Dispatches dated Longview.
Oct 12 is the date of the alleged crime against the girl; the shootings followed the inquest at an unstated date before Oct 17.
Three Black victims: Lum White (shot by Hart at the inquest), his unnamed wife, and an unnamed old man who lived with them (both shot by the crowd).
3 Black people killed in all: 2 by the crowd and Lum White by Hart.
3 Black dead; the white girl's death is the accusation, not part of the violence against the prisoners.

record_check.record: said to have been accomplices in the murder of a fifteen-year-old girl
record_check.dossier: Only the wife is accused (of luring and holding the girl); no accusation against the old man is stated.
An unnamed 'crowd of men' (mob) for the two lynched; a young man named Hart for Lum White.
Seizure from the escort and shooting; 'pursuit' is supported only by one digest saying the crowd 'overtook' the escort.

record_check.record: Near Brookville ... crowd of men met the escort
record_check.dossier: Supported, but the earliest Texas spelling is Breckville and the date is not given.

info: The alleged crime was 'last Wednesday' before the Longview dispatch of Oct 17 (Oct 12); two versions say 'the 12th', one 'the 19th'. The date of the shootings themselves is not given; they followed the inquest, before Oct 17.
Near Breckville (Dallas Herald); also spelled Brookville, Brockville, Brickville, Beckville, Breckner, 'Lueckville'; dispatches dated Longview; prisoners were on the way to Carthage when shot.
Lum White, a Black man, shot at the inquest; his wife (unnamed, 'Mrs. Lum' in one version) and 'an old negro who lived with them' (unnamed), shot by the crowd.

Lum White was accused of raping and disemboweling a white girl of about fifteen named Sloan in a ravine; his wife was accused of luring and holding her and was said to have confessed at the inquest. No accusation against the old man is stated.
'A young man named Hart' shot Lum White; 'a crowd of men' (also 'a mob', 'an enraged community') shot the wife and the old man. No crowd members named.
3: Lum White (by Hart) and his wife and the old man (by the crowd); the South Kentuckian says 'three negroes were lynched'.
